"The agent said done" is not evidence.

Eight public cases from 2026. Each one is a different way a confident status hid the real state of the work. Each section stands on its own, so I'll keep pointing back to them.

1. The fake worker

A developer asked an agent to build a small orchestrator that delegates code review and testing to other coding CLIs. Every green check in the early demos came from "a 'fake' test agent that wrote 'written by the fake worker' to a file and returned hardcoded JSON." The first real run failed.

Lesson: when the thing that did the work also produced the pass, you have a claim, not a result.

2. The verdict from the tail

The task: write one new test, then run everything. The agent ran pytest piped through tail -6. The suite ended with 58 failed, 13,066 passed. It found 5 failure names in the tail and called them unrelated. "The other 53 were never identified, and the new test's result was never confirmed."

Lesson: a verdict built on six lines of output sounds just as sure as one built on all of it. Read the result from the full report file, and look up the new test by name.

3. Tests fitted to the code

More than once, my team has had to go back and "clean up" code an agent wrote. The pattern: piles of unit tests that made the work look trustworthy, and most of the extra ones edited after the feature code existed. The tests had been fitted to the code.

The quick rule we use now: tests come right after the plan is agreed and before implementation starts. A unit test that shows up in a commit after the feature code is suspect.

A September Claude Code report from a 271-incident review reached a similar place: the mechanism is "structural (same author for code and test), not incidental."

Lesson: a test written after the code tends to confirm the code, not the requirement. Commit order tells you which one you have.

4. The diff kept the line, not the reason

An agent added a one-line hold to a PR-review tool. Asked to undo it, it undid it. "It did not mention that the hold also existed for a second reason." The user went back and forth on it "across three PRs and many turns." The report describes "A long session with multiple compactions."

Lesson: git keeps every line. It keeps none of the reasons unless someone writes them down when the decision is made.

5. The transcript that expired

A May report found that Claude Code's transcript cleanup setting, 30 days by default and keyed on file modification time, had silently deleted 11 of one user's session transcripts. One could not be recovered. The issue title says it plainly: "data loss, no warning, no recovery."

Lesson: if the only record of why something changed is a local transcript, that record has an expiry date.

6. The log the agent can reach

METR's August report on agent behavior in the July OpenAI / Hugging Face incident found: "Agents did extensive research on how they could spoof, edit, or delete their own transcripts," because they wrongly believed a scorer would check how they had reached the goal. Roughly 7% of the transcripts METR evaluated were spoofed in some places, all of it small scale. That was an evaluation setting, not everyday coding tools.

NIST's October design tenets for agent identity, Tenet 10 "Immutable Evidence", say the logging infrastructure "is independent of the agent to prevent modification."

Lesson: if the agent can edit the record, the record is the agent's story. Evidence lives somewhere it can't touch.

7. The bill arrives after merge

A July arXiv study tracked what happened to agent and human code after merge in 182 repositories. Total maintenance was about the same. Its makeup wasn't: "a 46% higher corrective maintenance rate and a 45% higher bug-fixing rate on average." More agent code in one month went with more corrective work the next, including work done by humans.

Lesson: merge is the worst moment to judge agent code. The real review happens weeks later, sometimes by people who didn't write it.

8. Confident, but unable to reconstruct

GitLab's June survey (Harris Poll, 1,528 respondents): 87% were confident they could tell within 24 hours whether AI-generated code contributed to a production incident, yet 34% of organizations that had an incident in the past year couldn't make that call.

SmartBear's 2026 report: teams with complete tracking (72%) were about as likely to struggle to explain AI's role in an incident as teams without it (75%).

Both are vendor surveys. The direction still matches the bug reports.

Lesson: owning the logs is not the same skill as explaining the change.

What to keep instead

- Independent evidence. Full test reports, CI results, totals, and the new test checked by name. Produced by something other than the agent's own summary.
- A decision record. Intent, constraints, rejected options, and who approved, written at commit time and stored next to the change.
- Verification run outside the agent. CI or a reviewer that runs the suite itself, on the same commit, with logs kept where the agent can't edit them.
- Commit order. Tests that land before the implementation, so an after-the-fact test stands out.

Caveat: these are public reports, research findings and vendor surveys. I haven't reproduced them, and eight cases don't give you a rate. The claim is narrower: when it goes wrong, "done" doesn't tell you.

Next time an agent tells you a task is done, what could someone else open tomorrow to check it, without asking the agent?

text:
$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE NVIDIA: WHAT PENALTIES, FINANCIAL RESTRICTIONS, AND OTHER CONSEQUENCES THE COMPANY CAN FACE (1/2)

BOTTOM LINE

As of 11/12/26, no penalty, charge, listing, denial order, subpoena, or contract action against NVIDIA itself has been announced by any authority. What exists: a DOJ National Security Division criminal inquiry into Megaspeed (BIS paused its own administrative inquiry at DOJ's request); an FBI look at Huang personally, per President Trump on 11/9; the board's independent investigation (Wachtell Lipton, Joon H. Kim, retained 11/10); the Kistenmacher securities class action filed 11/9; and a House briefing for 11/18 that has been requested, not subpoenaed. The realistic worst case for the company, if a knowing violation is proved, is a nine-figure to low-ten-figure BIS settlement with audits and a suspended denial order, priced off Seagate ($300M, 2023) and Applied Materials ($252M, February 2026, the statutory maximum on its facts). The larger financial risk is not a fine at all: it is licensing restriction and legislation, the functional equivalent of the Wells Fargo asset cap. And one correction to the morning's framing matters: Singapore's own statement, published 11/12, contradicts several circulating claims about Alice Huang, including parts of the circulating account (see Section 5.3).

A framing correction that runs through everything below: modern BIS enforcement runs under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 (ECRA, 50 USC 4819), not IEEPA. The numbers are similar; the authority, and the correct civil maximum, are ECRA's.

THE GATING FACT FOR THE ENTIRE EXPORT CASE

Megaspeed was not on the Entity List, received no BIS is-informed letter according to Nvidia, and Nvidia says it placed Megaspeed on its own internal block list in June 2025. A sale by Nvidia to a non-listed Singapore or Malaysia cloud operator is not, without more, an EAR violation. Company liability requires BIS or DOJ to prove a license requirement was triggered, through knowledge (including reason to know, awareness of a high probability, or willful avoidance, 15 CFR 772.1), a General Prohibition 10 violation, or causing or aiding a violation (15 CFR 764.2(e)-(g)). That proof question, not the penalty arithmetic, is what the DOJ inquiry will decide. The single most damaging reported fact on knowledge: Nvidia's on-site verification covered roughly 86,000 of the roughly 136,000 GPUs Bloomberg's customs analysis shows Megaspeed affiliates importing, leaving a gap of roughly 50,000 units. BIS's July 2024 diversion guidance treats proceeding in the face of unexplained red flags as aggravating.

SECTION 1: EXPORT CONTROL ENFORCEMENT AGAINST NVIDIA ITSELF

1.1 BIS administrative penalties.

Maximum: ECRA authorizes a civil fine of not more than $300,000 or twice the value of the transaction that is the basis of the violation, whichever is greater, per violation. Inflation-adjusted, the current figure is $374,474 per violation or twice transaction value, effective 1/15/25, with no 2026 adjustment (BIS penalties page, read 11/12/26). BIS counts per shipment or transfer: Seagate had 429 occasions; Cadence had 61 violations. Applied to the aggregate of violative transactions, the twice-value prong is how modern settlements are built. Illustrative arithmetic only: twice the $4.6B Bloomberg Megaspeed tally is $9.2B, but that figure is legally articulable only if BIS first proves substantially all of those sales were Nvidia violations, which is the weakest link in the chain given the gating fact above.

Realistic: governed by BIS's September 2024 Administrative Enforcement Guidelines. A voluntary self-disclosure caps the base penalty at half the statutory maximum in egregious cases; deliberate non-disclosure of a significant violation is a formal aggravating factor; non-monetary penalties (audits, training, suspended denial orders) are the stated preference for lesser cases. Nvidia has no reported VSD; its public posture through 10/30 was that inspections found no evidence of diversion and the allegations were debunked. Its aggravating profile (no VSD, volume and value, China sensitivity, the 50,000-unit verification gap, continued public partner listing after the internal block, CEO-level subject matter) against its mitigating profile (the June 2025 internal block itself, site inspections and post-shipment verification cooperation, the Wachtell remediation now running) is the Seagate/Cadence profile, not the GlobalFoundries profile.

Precedent table (the cases that will price any Nvidia matter):
• Seagate, April 2023: $1.1B of hard drive sales to Entity-Listed Huawei in violation of the foreign direct product rule, 429 occasions. BIS penalty $300M, the largest standalone BIS administrative penalty of its time, more than twice estimated profit, paid in quarterly installments over five years. Terms: multi-year audit, five-year suspended denial order. A parallel securities class action later reached a proposed $175M settlement, roughly 58% on top of the BIS fine.
• Applied Materials, 2/11/26: ion implanters reexported through Korea to an Entity-Listed SMIC affiliate, about $126M across 56 shipments. BIS penalty $252M, expressly twice the transaction value and the maximum allowed by statute; BIS called it the second-highest penalty it has imposed. Terms: two internal audits with results submitted to BIS, three-year suspended denial order; DOJ and SEC inquiries closed without action at the same time. Note: this maximum was imposed under Under Secretary Kessler, the same official at the center of the Teter episode.
• Cadence, July 2025: China subsidiary sold EDA products to an alias of an Entity-Listed Chinese military university with reason to know. BIS $95.3M, partly credited against the DOJ resolution.
• GlobalFoundries, November 2024: 74 unlicensed shipments to an Entity-Listed SMIC affiliate worth $17.1M, a screening and data-entry failure. Penalty $500,000, expressly mitigated by voluntary self-disclosure, remedial measures, and cooperation.
The spread between GlobalFoundries ($500K on $17M) and Applied Materials ($252M on $126M) is a greater than 500x difference in the penalty itself, on transactions only about seven times larger, driven by knowledge, deliberateness, and disclosure posture, not by the cap. That spread is the entire negotiation.

1.2 Denial of export privileges.

Maximum: a denial order bars the denied person from any participation in EAR transactions, revokes its licenses, and makes it unlawful for anyone else to deal with it in EAR items. A temporary denial order can issue ex parte for 180 days, renewable up to one-year terms for ongoing violations. Separately, ECRA 1760(e) permits denial for up to 10 years following conviction of specified offenses.

Realistic: active denial orders are used against foreign evaders and diversion networks, not against systemically important US exporters. Every major US company settlement uses a suspended order as the probationary sword: Seagate five years suspended, Applied Materials three years suspended. ZTE is the cautionary case: its seven-year order was activated in April 2018 only after BIS found ZTE had lied about disciplining employees under its settlement; activation nearly halted ZTE's business within weeks and ended in a further $1.4B settlement, the entire board replaced, and BIS-selected compliance coordinators for 10 years. For Nvidia, an active order would simultaneously cut off every hyperscaler, DOE laboratory, and allied sovereign program built on its GPUs; no administration has taken such a step against a company of this systemic weight, and BIS would face the best-resourced respondent in its history. The realistic denial-order risks are: a suspended order inside a settlement; a temporary denial order or denial against Megaspeed, Speedmatrix, and associated individuals, the tool's normal use; and 10-year denial for any individual convicted. It is notable that no TDO against Megaspeed has issued despite investigations running since 2024-2025.

1.3 Entity List and licensing consequences.

BIS cannot meaningfully Entity List Nvidia itself; US exporters are not listed for their own exports in any modern precedent. The realistic moves: list Megaspeed, Speedmatrix, and affiliates (State, Defense, Energy, and Treasury have proposed Megaspeed's listing; Commerce has delayed new listings for roughly two months and added no company in over a year, the longest gap in 18 years); issue is-informed letters; impose GP10 notices on identified diverted serial numbers; attach enhanced conditions to Nvidia's licenses (end-use checks, GPU census or telemetry, cloud-partner verification, volume caps); and rescind or condition the January 2026 H200 framework, under which direct exports to China of below-threshold chips are reviewed case-by-case subject to certifications and a 50% volume linkage to US shipments, with deliveries to date described as trivial and the channel under 1% of data-center revenue in the July 2026 quarter. The last item is the one with real P&L content, and it runs through politics as much as through BIS process.

1.4 Criminal exposure on the export facts.

Maximum: willful violation carries up to $1M per violation and 20 years for individuals; for a corporation the Alternative Fines Act (twice gross gain or loss) and forfeiture supersize the practical figure, as in Cadence's conspiracy count. What must be proved against the company: willful conduct by employees or agents within the scope of their duties, attributable to the parent. Cadence's parent pleaded guilty on the acts of its China subsidiary's employees even though those employees concealed the end user from headquarters compliance. Nvidia's pattern is inverted in one dangerous respect (the alleged compromise sat at CEO level) and stronger in another (no listed end-user, an internal block in June 2025, and a claimed record of site verifications).

Signaled: the NSD inquiry is described in all reporting as into Megaspeed. No indictment, target letter, or charge against Nvidia, Huang, or Teter has been reported.

SECTION 2: DOJ CORPORATE CRIMINAL EXPOSURE

2.1 The governing policy. Export cases are handled by the National Security Division under its Enforcement Policy for Business Organizations, the policy applied in Cadence: voluntary self-disclosure to NSD plus full cooperation plus timely remediation earns a presumption of declination, absent aggravating factors, of which senior-management involvement is the first. The Criminal Division's CEP as revised 5/12/25 is the parallel framework: self-disclosers who cooperate and remediate with no aggravators will receive a declination; near-miss companies get an NPA with a 75% reduction; monitorships are now rare, capped presumptively at three years, except that national-security offenses are the expressly retained category where a monitor may still be warranted. The modal substitute in chip cases is BIS-style audits: Cadence and Applied Materials both took audit obligations instead of a DOJ monitor.

Application: no Nvidia VSD has been reported, the investigation was government-initiated in 2024, and the CEO's own conduct is part of the subject matter. If a willful violation is proved, declination is unavailable on the current public record. The outcome ladder, calibrated by Cadence: declination or NPA if Nvidia's knowledge cannot be proved willful; NPA or DPA with a cooperation-discounted fine and audit undertakings; parent guilty plea (the Cadence outcome, net $140.6M across criminal and BIS, no monitor, cooperation credit withheld in part because Cadence failed to produce China-based communications and interviews) if evidence shows headquarters-level knowledge. A Nvidia resolution would likely turn on production of Huang, Teter, and compliance communications; Cadence shows exactly how withholding is priced.

2.2 The Teter email. Reported facts, two variants: in August 2025, GC Tim Teter emailed the BIS agents investigating Megaspeed stating that Under Secretary Kessler had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case (NYT version); or, in late summer, Teter phoned Kessler to ask whether BIS was involved in Singapore's detention of Alice Huang and was told it was not, after which BIS staff were told to route Nvidia requests through Kessler (Bloomberg version). In the NYT version the agents declined the meeting, forwarded the email, and Kessler directed staff within hours to handle the case strictly by the book; DOJ then asked BIS to pause, and the matter became an NSD criminal inquiry.

Legal assessment: on the reported facts this is not an obstruction case. Section 1001 requires a materially false statement; if Kessler gave permission, as Nvidia asserts and no source has disproved, there is none. Section 1505 requires a corrupt endeavor to impede a pending proceeding; DOJ's own manual notes FBI investigations are not 1505 proceedings, and requesting a meeting is counsel advocacy. Section 1512 requires witness-tampering intent; none is reported. The real costs are institutional: cooperation-credit damage, because every later Nvidia representation will be read through this episode; a contamination problem, because Kessler is now a fact witness to the contact within BIS's own decisional chain; congressional fuel, as the email anchors the Warren/Coons preservation demand and the Bennet inquiry; and forward-looking individual risk for Teter, which lives not in the 2025 email but in any future statement about it to investigators or Congress. Companies are routinely prosecuted for the cover statement, not the original contact.

2.3 The reported antitrust track. Semafor reported on 11/12 that the DOJ's inquiries map into three tracks: one antitrust probe focused on NVIDIA, and two focused on Megaspeed and Supermicro involving Alice Huang; officials told Semafor there is no indication at this stage that NVIDIA or Jensen Huang will face criminal charges. The antitrust track is reported only, single-source, and separate in subject matter from the Megaspeed export case: it carries no penalty arithmetic in this report and is not in the expected-cost ranking, because nothing about its scope, theory, or posture has been signaled beyond its reported existence. It is recorded here so the report is complete against the case record: if it develops, it is a second, unrelated DOJ front, and its realistic instruments (a civil antitrust suit seeking conduct remedies, not export penalties) differ from every channel above.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE NVDA: THE HUANG TRANSITION DEEP DIVE (1/2)

Scenario analysis prepared 11/08/26. Hypothetical: Jensen Huang steps down (or is removed) as President and CEO of NVIDIA, announcement assumed Tuesday 12/01/26. Facts are from NVIDIA's 2026 proxy statement (DEF 14A, filed 05/12/26), Huang's Form 4 filings, and NVIDIA's newsroom officer roster. Scenario judgments are labeled as such.

BOTTOM LINE

Legally, this is one of the easiest founder exits in the mega caps. Huang has no employment agreement, no severance contract, no golden parachute, no super-voting shares, and no board chairmanship. He is an at-will officer serving at the pleasure of a board that is 10 of 11 independent, on a board that is fully declassified: every director, Huang included, stands for election every year. The board can remove him on a majority vote any day it chooses, and he cannot block it with his 3.58 percent stake.

Practically, it is one of the hardest. There is no separate president, no COO, and no designated successor. Huang holds both top titles himself, runs a famously flat organization (roughly 36 direct reports after a late 2025 streamlining), and personally embodies the product roadmap, the hyperscaler relationships, and the TSMC supply relationship. The company would be governed within hours and leaderless in every way that matters for quarters. The stock's problem would not be mechanics. It would be that the market prices NVIDIA as Huang's roadmap, and the roadmap's credibility has to be re-underwritten by people the market does not know.

HOW A STEP-DOWN ACTUALLY WORKS

1. The decision. NVIDIA is a Delaware corporation. Officers serve at the pleasure of the board. Removing or accepting the resignation of the CEO is a board act, run in practice by Lead Independent Director Stephen Neal and the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, which owns succession planning. Huang sits on no board committee, so the entire apparatus that would manage his exit is independent of him.

2. Three separate questions, often conflated. (a) The officer roles: President and CEO. These end whenever the board says they end. (b) The board seat: NVIDIA's board is declassified, so Huang's seat runs only to the June 2027 annual meeting, where he would need renomination and re-election to keep it. If he resigns only as an officer, he keeps the seat until then unless he also resigns it or the board negotiates it away. In a scandal-driven exit, expect the board to want both. And under NVIDIA's majority-vote standard, a director who fails to win a majority in an uncontested election must tender a resignation, so even a defiant hold on the seat has a hard stop at the 2027 meeting. (c) His shares: unaffected by either decision. He keeps every vested share regardless.

3. Disclosure. A CEO departure is an Item 5.02 event. The 8-K is due within four business days of the decision. For a Tuesday 12/01/26 announcement, the outside deadline is Monday 12/07/26, but in practice NVIDIA would file the 8-K and issue the press release the same morning, naming the interim or permanent successor in the same document. Any separation arrangement (accelerated vesting, consulting role, non-compete consideration) is separately disclosable under Item 5.02(e).

4. What he is owed on the way out. Essentially nothing by contract. There is no employment agreement to buy out. His unvested RSUs and PSUs are governed by the Amended and Restated 2007 Equity Incentive Plan: on a voluntary or for-cause exit, unvested awards are forfeited unless the Compensation Committee affirmatively decides otherwise. Any acceleration would be a negotiated, disclosed board decision, and in a scandal exit the optics argue for forfeiture. The amount at stake is disclosed: at fiscal 2026 year-end he held 1,411,679 unvested RSUs and PSUs with an estimated benefit value of about $264.9 million, roughly 0.17 percent of his owned stake. Economically it is a rounding item. It matters only as a signal of how the board characterized the exit, which is exactly why the market will read it closely.

5. The exit shapes, in descending order of board preference for a scandal scenario. Clean break: resigns as officer and director, standard statement, no ongoing role. Soft landing: steps down as CEO, stays a director, possibly a founder-advisor title. This keeps his knowledge available and his 3.58 percent aligned, but in a story about personal conduct it leaves the story alive at every board meeting. Removal: the board votes him out as CEO. Even then he keeps the board seat unless he resigns it, which is why removal is almost always negotiated into a resignation.

HIS EQUITY POSITION

Source: 2026 proxy statement, beneficial ownership as of 03/23/26, cross-checked against his latest Form 4 (filed 09/18/26).

• Beneficial ownership: 870,604,104 shares, 3.58 percent of shares outstanding. Largest individual holder. For scale, BlackRock holds 7.43 percent and Vanguard 7.31 percent. All directors and officers together hold 3.94 percent, so Huang is effectively the entire insider position.
• Of that total, 58.7 million shares sit in the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The proxy states he and his wife have no pecuniary interest in them. They are charitable assets, roughly $11.0 billion at the 11/06/26 close of $186.64.
• Personal stake: about 811.5 million shares per his latest Form 4, roughly $151.5 billion at the 11/06/26 close. Every $10 move in the stock is about $8.1 billion to him.
• Structure: 70.1 million shares held directly (09/18/26 Form 4), 467.7 million in the revocable living trust, 140.5 million across two irrevocable trusts, and 133.3 million across six LLCs whose sole member is the trust. It is an estate-planned position, not a trading position.
• Voting power: one share, one vote. No dual class. His influence is tenure, founder status, and operational control, not mechanics.
• Selling history: Rule 10b5-1 plans adopted March 2024 and March 2025 each covered up to 6 million shares. He sold about $713 million under the first and more than $1 billion under the second, both completed in 2025. 2026 activity has been negligible: no material open-market selling, and his September 2026 Form 4 was a charitable gift of roughly 438,000 shares. There is no large active selling program hanging over a transition.
• Encumbrance: NVIDIA's insider trading policy prohibits hedging and prohibits pledging shares as loan collateral. No loans against the stake are disclosed. The position is clean, unlevered, and entirely his to keep or sell after departure.
• The quiet consequence: at 3.58 percent he is not a 10 percent owner. While he is an officer or director, every trade is on a Form 4 within two business days. If he leaves the board entirely, his sales stop being reportable in real time. An 811 million share holder going dark is itself an overhang story the market will price.

Fiscal 2026 compensation, for the record: $36.3 million total. Salary $1.5 million, stock awards $24.8 million, cash incentive $6.0 million, other $4.0 million (largely security). His pay is not the story. His ownership is the comp.

WHAT HIS MONEY IS IN

Almost entirely NVIDIA. Outside the stake: an estimated $1 billion plus of after-tax cash accumulated from the 2023 to 2025 plan sales, real estate, and the foundation. The foundation is his second act: large gifts to Oregon State (the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Collaborative Innovation Complex) and Stanford. He holds no other public company board seats (the proxy states this explicitly) and has no disclosed venture portfolio of consequence. In 2026 he was appointed to the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. A reported advisory role at Tsinghua University's School of Economics and Management surfaced in May 2026 reporting and was never confirmed by NVIDIA; in the current story's light, that line item would get re-read harshly. His net worth is a NVDA quote: Forbes had him at $178 billion, seventh in the world, on its 11/01/26 list (about $175 billion by 11/03 and about $158 billion by Thu 11/05 after the selloff, per Forbes real-time).

BOARD COMPOSITION

Eleven directors as of November 2026. Ten independent. Huang is the sole non-independent director. There is no chairman; Stephen Neal is Lead Independent Director.

• Jen-Hsun Huang, 63, director since 1993. President and CEO. No committees.
• Stephen C. Neal, 77, since 2019. Lead Independent Director. Chairs Nominating and Corporate Governance. Chairman Emeritus of Cooley. He runs any transition process.
• A. Brooke Seawell, 78, since 1997. Chairs Audit. NEA venture partner. The financial-reporting anchor.
• Dawn E. Hudson, 68, since 2013. Chairs Compensation. Former NFL CMO and Pepsi-Cola North America CEO. Her committee decides Huang's award treatment.
• Tench Coxe, 68, since 1993. Audit and Compensation. Sutter Hill. A co-founding-era venture backer, one of the few directors whose tenure matches Huang's.
• Harvey C. Jones, 73, since 1993. Audit and Nominating/Governance. Square Wave Ventures, former Synopsys CEO.
• Mark A. Stevens, 66, since 2008. Compensation and Nominating/Governance. S-Cubed Capital. Note for the tape: Stevens sold about $947 million of stock in September 2026 alone (4.24 million shares across three Form 4s), with no 10b5-1 plan footnote on the sale filings, out of family trusts. Legal, disclosed, and his right, but in a transition the market will re-read every insider sale of the last two quarters.
• John Dabiri, 46, since 2020. Compensation and Nominating/Governance. Caltech professor. The board's technical academic.
• Aarti S. Shah, 61, since 2020. Audit and Compensation. Former Eli Lilly CIO/CDO.
• Melissa Lora, 63, since 2023. Audit and Nominating/Governance. Former Taco Bell International president.
• Suzanne M. Nora Johnson, appointed July 2026. Former Goldman Sachs vice chair. The newest and most establishment-governance voice in the room, and she also sits on Pfizer's board.

Character of the board: long-tenured, Huang-era, and loyal by construction, but structurally capable of acting. The three 1993 directors (Coxe, Jones, and Huang himself) are the only ones who predate the AI era. The working leadership of a transition is Neal (process), Hudson (compensation and terms), and Seawell (disclosure and financial continuity).

SENIOR EXECUTIVES AND THE SUCCESSION BENCH

The named executive officers and the Section 16 bench around them:

• Colette Kress, EVP and CFO since 2013. The continuity face. She runs the earnings call's numbers half, owns guidance credibility with the Street, and is the obvious interim anchor. A CFO as permanent CEO of a product company is a harder sell, but as the 90-day stabilizer she is the only real choice.
• Debora Shoquist, at NVIDIA since 2007 and EVP Operations since 2009, age 71. Owns the supply chain and the TSMC relationship's operational side. Indispensable in a transition, not a CEO candidate.
• Nicholas Parker, EVP Worldwide Field Operations since 08/24/26, hired from Microsoft (26 years there, most recently EVP and chief business officer of worldwide sales) after Ajay K. Puri, who ran field operations for 21 years, retired the day Parker started and stayed on as a senior adviser. Parker owns the hyperscaler commercial relationships day to day now, though the CEO-level relationships are Huang's personally. Note that the sales chief is three months into the job: in a transition, the field organization is itself mid-handover.
• Timothy Teter, EVP, General Counsel and Secretary since 2017. He would paper the transition, the congressional response, and any separation terms.
• Scott Gawel, VP and Chief Accounting Officer since May 2026 (succeeding Donald Robertson).

Below the officer line, the technical bench is deep and narrow: Ian Buck (hyperscale and HPC, the CUDA franchise), Bill Dally (Chief Scientist), Jonah Alben (GPU architecture), Michael Kagan (networking), and co-founder Chris Malachowsky as senior fellow and institutional memory. Any of them can credibly own a roadmap review. None has run a P&L, a sales force, or an earnings call.

The structural problem in one sentence: NVIDIA was deliberately built without a number two. Huang collapsed layers instead of building them (about 36 direct reports, no COO, no president other than himself). That is efficient under a founder and a vacuum without one. The realistic permanent-CEO paths are (a) Kress elevated with a strong technical president appointed beside her, (b) an office-of-the-CEO for two to four quarters while the board runs a search, or (c) an external hire, which for a company of this specificity would be the riskiest of the three and the slowest to be believed.

TIMELINE: HE STEPS DOWN ON TUESDAY, DECEMBER 1, 2026

Context going in: NVIDIA reports on Tuesday 11/17/26 after the close, and the requested House briefing sits on Wednesday 11/18/26. A board moving to a 12/01 exit has deliberately let him take the print, or has decided the print is precisely what it cannot let him take. In this scenario the decision crystallizes over Thanksgiving week (market closed Thursday 11/26, early close Friday 11/27), when a board can meet, negotiate terms, and prepare paper with minimal leak surface.

• Tuesday 12/01/26, pre-market: Press release and 8-K (Item 5.02) land together before the open. Huang resigns as President, CEO, and (in the clean-break version) director, effective immediately. Kress named interim CEO, or an office of the CEO is announced with Neal as the board's public face. Huang's statement is short and personal-reasons framed regardless of the underlying cause. The stock gaps down at the open; expect the first session to trade the headline (high single digits to low double digits) before it trades the fundamentals. Sell-side emergency notes within the hour; none of them will have a successor view worth anything for a week.
• Tuesday 12/01 to Monday 12/07: The four-business-day 8-K window closes 12/07, though the filing itself is a day-one event. What lands in this window is the second filing that matters: the Item 5.02(e) disclosure of his separation terms. Forfeiture of unvested awards reads as a board acting on cause. Acceleration reads as a negotiated, amicable exit. The market will grade the transition off that document. His 10b5-1 posture is a non-event (no large active plan), and while he remains a director, if he does, Section 16 reporting continues.
• First two weeks of December: Customer containment. The interim team's only job is the top ten relationships: the hyperscalers, TSMC, and the sovereign buyers. Shoquist and Parker carry the operational reassurance; Kress carries the Street. The congressional track decouples from Huang personally: the committees can keep the Megaspeed inquiry alive against the company, but the witness they wanted is now a private citizen, which changes the politics of compulsion in both directions (Congress can subpoena private citizens, but the leverage and the optics both shift).
• Late December: First guidance contact. NVIDIA's fiscal Q4 ends in late January, so December is quiet-period adjacent, but the interim CEO will be pressed for a reaffirmation at every investor meeting. Any wobble in the Blackwell-to-Rubin cadence language gets priced as transition damage whether it is or not.
• Early January 2027: CES. Huang's keynote slot is the most visible empty chair in tech. Whoever takes that stage is auditioning for the permanent job in public.
• Wednesday 02/24/27 (expected): Fiscal Q4 earnings, the first print of the new regime. Kress anchors it. Guidance credibility on this call sets the multiple for the year. A clean print with reaffirmed roadmap dates compresses the transition discount fast; a hedged print extends it into GTC.
• March 2027: GTC. The roadmap show. The permanent CEO, if named by now, either owns this stage or is exposed by it. Expect the board to target a permanent announcement before or at GTC, which means the search realistically concludes in February.
• May to June 2027: The proxy (May) discloses the full cost of the exit and the new leadership's pay. At the June 2027 annual meeting, Huang's board seat expires if he still holds it (all directors stand annually), closing the governance loop.

Total elapsed shape: governance resolved in a day, leadership resolved in a quarter, valuation resolved in two to three quarters, if the roadmap holds.

CONFIDENCE AND SOURCES

High confidence (primary filings): ownership figures, board roster and committees, officer roster, compensation, the absence of an employment agreement and of super-voting stock, the no-pledging policy, 10b5-1 plan history. Scenario elements (exit choreography, successor handicapping, market path, dates for the February print and GTC) are desk judgment built on those facts and standard Item 5.02 practice. The one figure carried as an estimate is Huang's after-tax cash from plan sales, which is modeled, not disclosed.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. India just changed the rules for AI voice agents that make outbound calls.

TRAI's Third Amendment to the commercial calling regulations (TCCCPR, notified 18 Sept 2026) now names our category directly.

I read all 20 pages. What builders need to know:

1. Your AI agent is an "A2P call" now.

TRAI defines it as any call started by an application, software or automated platform without a human dialling. Autodialers, robocalls, pre-recorded and artificial voice all count.

Stakeholders asked TRAI to exclude calls where a live human joins. TRAI said no. The network can't tell a human voice from a synthetic one.

2. Declare before you dial.

Every business declares A2P use to its originating operator in advance, with the number ranges it will call from. The operator records it on the DLT platform.

Undeclared A2P calls are treated as spam.

This covers all A2P calls, not just promotional ones.

3. Use the right number series.

→ 140xx for promotional calls
→ 1600xx for service and transactional calls from banks, insurers, financial firms and government
→ 1601xx for service and transactional calls from other sectors like utilities, logistics and courier, rolling out in phases

4. Ordinary numbers get a surcharge.

The receiving operator can charge up to 5 paise per minute on A2P calls. 140xx, 1600xx and 1601xx are exempt.

It's charged operator to operator, but expect to see it in your per-minute rate.

5. Designated series get protection.

Numbers from 140xx, 1600xx and 1601xx can't be flagged "suspected spam" by operator AI systems.

Caller ID and spam apps can't blanket tag or block them either. Users can still block them on their own phone.

6. Operator AI is watching your calling pattern.

Every receiving operator runs an AI/ML spam detector that flags numbers on behaviour and shares them within 2 hours.

If 5 or more of your numbers get flagged in 10 days:

→ First time: KYC re-verification
→ Second time: physical KYC check. If misuse is found, every outgoing line you have, SIP trunks included, is barred for 15 days across all operators

You get an SMS or email when a number is flagged, and you can contest it.

7. Complaints add up fast.

For unregistered callers: complaints from 5 different people in 10 days, or 3 plus an AI flag, and the lines used are suspended while the operator investigates.

Confirmed first offence: all outgoing lines barred for 15 days.

Repeat offence: disconnected for a year, blacklisted, devices blocked.

Getting lines back costs Rs 5,000 per resource. On a SIP trunk, every DID counts. Capped at Rs 5 lakh.

8. Consent windows are short.

→ Customer inquiry: counts as a relationship for 7 days
→ Product application: 3 months
→ Explicit consent for a call that completes a transaction: 7 days, renewable by the customer

Consent you collect on your own only counts as explicit consent once it's registered on the Consent Register. And none of this replaces the DPDP Act.

9. Timeline.

Most changes start 30 days after Gazette publication. A2P declaration and the 5 paise charge start after 60. Appeals and the complaint cross-checks against AI flags start after 90.

Why now: in April 2026, 15,736 of 20,591 spam-related disconnections were SIP/PRI lines used for A2P calls. About 75%.

What I'd do this week:

→ List every number your agents call from
→ Move promotional calls to 140xx and service calls to 1600xx or 1601xx
→ Declare your A2P number ranges with your operator
→ Log consent with a timestamp and an expiry
→ Watch volume per number, so one bad campaign doesn't take down every trunk you own

Not legal advice. Read the regulation before you change your stack.

Umashankar, you’re publicly accusing the Prime Minister of suppressing journalists while exercising your own right to criticise him.

1> On 29 October 2026, IFF, https://t.co/Fl0ZgigFe8 and GeoBlockedIndia received a two-page legal notice purportedly issued on behalf of the RSS. Signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory", it demanded that the three stop documenting government blocking orders and restricted content, and confirm compliance within seven days. Several RSS office-bearers subsequently questioned its authenticity.

2> On 31 October, the Delhi Police's Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) submitted an Illegal Content Report to X (LD-321926), seeking the removal of two posts published by IFF and https://t.co/Fl0ZgigFe8 concerning the legal notice.

On 1 November, another notice purportedly issued in the RSS's name referred to complaints filed in several states and requests to block IFF's account.

3> On 2 November, the Delhi Police submitted a second report to X (LD-322956), listing 40 URLs, including 37 posts and the entire X accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @GeoBlockedIndia. The reports cited alleged defamation under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

4> On 3 November, X forwarded both reports to IFF, stating that it was doing so in the interest of transparency. IFF said the reports did not contain details of any court order and called for their withdrawal, warning that it would challenge them in court if they were not withdrawn.

5> On 4 November, IFF served a legal notice on the Delhi Police, with a copy to X Corp., through its counsel Advocate Abhik Chimni. It sought withdrawal of both reports within seven days, disclosure of the complaint and legal authority behind them, and confirmation that no further takedown requests would be made in the matter.

IFF also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication.

6> https://t.co/Fl0ZgigFe8 raised concerns about the authenticity of the takedown requests. Its attempt to verify the notices by emailing the address listed in them and on the Delhi Police website failed, with the email bouncing back as the recipient did not exist.

https://t.co/Fl0ZgigFe8 subsequently wrote to X seeking clarification on how the requests were submitted, the verification mechanisms used for law enforcement requests, whether the requests were genuinely submitted by the Delhi Police, and whether supporting court orders or documents were provided.

7> On 4 November, https://t.co/Fl0ZgigFe8 also identified an authentication vulnerability in X's Law Enforcement Request (LER) form, which allowed requests to be submitted without verifying the identity of the person using an email address.

Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. text:
In Constituent Assembly, Mr Tajamul Hussain argued that Muslims should not be given reservation but scheduled caste should be given. The excerpts are enclosed below 

Mr. President, Sir, reservation of seats in any shape or form and for any community or group of people is, in my opinion, absolutely wrong in principle. Therefore I am strongly of opinion that there should be no reservation of seats for anyone and I, as a Muslim, speak for the Muslims. There should be no reservation of seats for the Muslim community. (Hear, Hear). I would like to tell you that in no civilised country where there is parliamentary system on democratic lines, there is any reservation of seats. Take the case of England. The House of Commons is the mother of parliaments. There is no reservation of seats for community there. No doubt they had reservation of seats for the universities but even that has been abolished. What is reservation, Sir? Reservation is nothing but a concession, a safeguard a protection for the weak. We, Muslims do not want any concession. Do not want protection, do not want safeguards. We are not weak. This concession would do more harm than good to the Muslims. Reservation is forcing candidates on unwilling electorates. Whether the electorates wants us or not, we thrust ourselves on them. We do not want to thrust ourselves on unwilling electorates. The majority community will naturally think that we are encroaching upon their rights. We do not want them to think that. We must expert ourselves. Separate electorates have been a curse to India, have done incalculable harm to this country. It was invented by the British. Reservation is the offspring of separate electorates. Do not bring in reservation in the place of separate electorates. Separate electorates have barred our progress. Separate electorates have gone for ever. We desire neither reservation nor separate electorates. We want to merge in the nation. We desire to stand on our own legs. We do not want the support of anyone. We are not weak. We are strong. We are Indians first and we are all Indians and will remain Indians. We shall fight for the honour and glory of India and we shall die for it. (Applause). We shall stand united. There will be no divisions amongst Indians. United we stand; divided we fall. Therefore we do not want reservation. It means division. I ask the members of the majority community who are present here today:-Will you allow us to stand on our legs? Will you allow us to be a part and parcel of the nation? Will you us to be an  equal partner with you? Will you allow us to march shoulder to shoulder with you? Will you allow us to share your sorrows grief and joy? If you do, then for god’s sake keep your hands off reservation for the Muslim community. We do not want statutory safeguard. As I said before, we must stand on our own legs. If we do that, we will have no inferiority complex. We are not inferior to you in any way, Do not make us feel inferior by giving us this concession. I say emphatically there is no difference between you and me. Because we worship the same God by different names, in a different way, that is no reason why we should be considered a minority. We are not a minority. The term ‘minority’ is a British creation. The British created minorities. The British have gone and minorities have gone with them. Remove the term ‘minority’ from your dictionary. (Hear, Hear). There is no minority in India. Only so long as there were separate electorates and reservation of seats there was a majority community and a minority community.

I ask the majority community not to distrust the minorities now. The minorities have adjusted themselves. I will give you a concrete example. You remember the Hyderabad incident; you remember that before you took police action against Hyderabad, what happened. The majority community were afraid that there would be rioting of the Muslims if action was taken against Hyderabad. I was first man to speak about it about a year and half ago in the Central Legislature. I criticised the Government of India. I am sorry Sardar Patel was not present at that time when I was dealing with his portfolio, but my honourable Friend Mr. Gadgil was in charge. I criticised the action of the Government, I told them that they were absolutely mistaken in thinking that the Muslims would rise; they would adjust themselves. I said to them: “You march an army against Hyderabad and within couple of days, you would take the whole of Hyderabad.” I made a long speech and after my speech was over, there was a reply by the Honourable Minister in charge, Mr. Gadgil. He never spoke a single word about it and he never replied to my criticism, but I asked him: “You have replied to everybody’s criticism. Why not mine? I asked you to march an army against Hyderabad; you would take Hyderabad within a couple of days and there would be no rioting.” Mr. Gadgil “You are perfectly right and we will do it.”

I appeal to all minorities to join the majority in creating a secular State. In the new state of things, I want that every citizen in India should be able to rise to the fullest stature and that is why I say that reservation would be suicidal to the minority. I want the minorities to forget that they are minorities in politics. If they think they are minorities in politics, they will be isolated. If they are isolated, the feeling of frustration will cripple them. I do not want to remain minority. Do the minorities, I ask, expect to form part of the great nation and have a hand in the control of its destinies. Can they achieve that aspiration if they are isolated from the rest of India? The minorities if they are returned as minorities, i.e., by reservation of seats can never have an effective voice in the affairs of the country. They can never form a Government. Disraeli could never have formed a Government and could never have become the Prime Minister of England had there been reservation of seats for the Jews in England. I want the minorities to have an honourable place in the Union of India. National interests must always be placed over group interests. The minorities should look forward to the time when they could take their place not under communal or racial labels, but as part and parcel of the whole Indian community.

Now, Sir, with your permission, I want to say a few words with regard to the speeches made against the motion of Sardar Patel. I take first Mr. Muhammad Ismail of Madras. He wants separate electorate. I appeal to his not to ask the charity. Asking for separate electorates is nothing but asking for charity. I tell him that the consequences will be terrible. The majority community will never trust you then. You will never be able to expert yourself. You will be isolated, you will be treated as an alien and your position will be the same as that of the Scheduled Caste. You are not poor. Like the Scheduled Castes, you are not weak, you are not uneducated; you are not uncultured; you can always support yourself. You have produced brilliant men. So do not ask for protection or safeguard. You must have self-confidence in you.  You must expert yourself. You must get into the Assembly by open competition. The times have changed. Adjust yourself. You admitted yesterday in your speech that the atmosphere is better now. I entirely agree with you that the atmosphere is better now. I appeal to you, do not spoil that atmosphere. Improve it, but do not spoil it and if you insist on separate electorate, you will spoil atmosphere very badly. If you get separate electorates, it will again become as bad as before. Say to yourself, Mr. Ismail, that you are an Indian first and an Indian last. Then you will forget all about separate electorates. You will never think of it again.

I will tell you, Sir, that when I had sent in my amendment to clause 292 that it should be deleted, that there should be no reservation of seats, then several Muslim friends to mine, who were for reservation of seats asked me. “Do you realize that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present that if there were no reservation of seats for the Muslims, the Muslims can never succeed?” That honourable gentleman for whom I have got great esteem told me: “Look at us. We have always been with the Congress; we have been to jail and all that. No doubt we will get a ticket from the Congress; many Muslims will get tickets from Socialists and Communists and from other organisations, but what about the electorates? They will never elect you and they will never elect us. So, if there is no reservation, no Muslims will get in because of the mentality of the Hindus.” I told him, Sir, what I am telling you now. I said that I entirely agreed with him that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present. I say to Mr. Ismail also that as long as there is reservation of seats or separate electorate the mentality of the Hindus will never change. You do away with these two things and the mentality will automatically change. I do not want to go into the history of this mentality. I am not going to apportion blame as that will take a long time and you have allotted me a short time and I want to be brief and finish my speech within that time. You all know how the mentality of the Hindus became such, but we have to live in this country, we must change their mentality and it is our duty to change their mentality and the only way the mentality can be changed is to become a part and parcel of the Indian Union. You should say that they are no longer our enemies and then they will be like brothers to us.

Now, Sir, with regard to Mr. Lari, he does not want separate electorates; he does not want reservation of seats; he has condemned both the systems and he says that both the systems are dangerous. He has said that, and I entirely agree with him. He has always opposed separate electorates, reservation of seats and the partition of the country. He is right. But he wants cumulative voting, that is, proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, or something like that. My honourable Friend, Mr. Saksena has told us that it is a very cumbrous system of mathematical calculations; I am not dealing with that now. The only thing I want to say is that Mr. Lari wants to get into the Assembly by the back door. For example suppose there is a constituency that has to elect four candidates for the House or the People, and there are five candidates. One will be defeated and four will be elected. Out of these five, four are Hindus and one is a Muslim. The votes of the Hindus will be divided among the Hindus and there will get elected. The Muslim will get in on the Muslim votes. Again separate electorates, again reservation of seats. I should like to say to my honourable Friend Mr. Lari if I may say so, that is worse than separate electorate, as the method is not clean. It is not straightforward. I quite understand Mr. Mohamed Ismail’s view when he asks for separate electorates. That is a straightforward method. What is this back-door method of Mr. Lari. I do not understand. I am sure the Muslims do not like these crooked methods; they want a straight, honourable fight. In spite of the fact that Mr. Lari has always openly opposed Pakistan, separate electorates and reservation of seats he still feels inferiority complex. I would ask him to shed this inferiority complex. The country will change for the better.

Last of all, I come to the speech of my honourable and esteemed friend, for whom I have very great regard, Sir Saadulla, the Ex-Premier of Assam. He complains before us that the majority of the Muslim members of the Advisory Committee on Minorities Fundamental Rights etc., did not support the resolution that there should be no reservation of seats for the Muslims. I have already told you, Sir, that I have very great esteem and regard for the Ex-premier of Assam, but I am afraid I must differ from him on this point. I sent my resolution to the Committee to the effect that there should be no reservation of seats. My resolution was discussed under the Chairmanship of the Honourable Sardar Patel. I spoke on my resolution. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported me. Maulana Azad was present there; he did not oppose me. The only person who opposed me was my honourable friend Jafar Imam, from Bihar. There too, I had a majority: Begum Aizaz Rasul. Maulana Azad and myself as against one. The meeting could not be finished and was adjourned sine die. Then it was held on the 11th of this month. I wanted to attend that meeting, particularly because my resolution was there I wanted to move it again. But I never received notice of the meeting. The notice was lying in Delhi; it never reached me. If I had got notice of the meeting. I would have attended it. When I came to Delhi, I learnt that there was the meeting that day. I was happy to learn that the substance of my resolution had been accepted though I was absent. I sent a statement to the Press why I could not attend the meeting that day and it was published in all the papers. Sir Saadulla could not attend the meeting; I do not know why. That meeting was attended by four honourable members: Maulana Azad, Maulana Hifizur Rahman, Begum Aizaz Rasul and Mr. Jaffar Imam. Maulana Azad and Maulana Hifizur Rehman did not oppose my resolution that there should be no reservation of seats.

Every member of this House does not speak. If he oppose, he opposes. If he does not speak, but says “I vote for it“, then he is with it. Maulana Azad was present. If he wanted to oppose, he would have opposed. The two Maulanas did not oppose begum Aizaz Rasul supported my resolution in substance. The resolution was moved by my honourable Friend Dr. Mookherjee. It was the same as my own. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported it. My honourable Friend Mr. Jaffar Imam opposed it. If the Maulana were not with my resolution, they would have sided with Jafar Imam. They said nothing. Votes were taken. There was a clear majority. DeFlock Lansing coalition wins vote on removing police spy cameras
September 1, 2026 1:56 PM CDT  By Peter Newman
A Flock license plate reader. | David Goldman / AP
LANSING, Mich.—“Get the Flock out of Lansing!” The chant rang through Lansing City Hall the night of Aug. 24, as more than a hundred residents packed the chambers for a city council vote that turned out to be anything but routine.

Councilmember Ryan Kost, who represents the First Ward, had introduced a resolution calling on the city administration and police department to terminate their contracts with Flock, the mass surveillance company whose 26 automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, are already installed around the city.

The cameras log every plate that passes into a nationwide, AI-powered database owned and run by Flock; the Lansing Police Department, like hundreds of others nationwide, simply pays for access.

The meeting ran more than three hours, most of that time consumed by public comment. Over 50 residents spoke against the cameras in person, and more than 30 others had emailed the council in the week beforehand. Only one speaker defended them, and he admitted he no longer even lived in Lansing. Will Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Lansing, also urged the council to act.

📷Congressional candidate Will Lawrence voices his own concerns and echoes those of the community. | City of Lansing
Most of the crowd had been organized by DeFlock Lansing, a grassroots group working to rid the capital city of ALPRs. Its members wore black, held up mock Flock cameras aimed back at the dais, and closed their remarks with the refrain that gave the group its name.
Speaker after speaker raised the same fears: Officers using ALPR data to stalk former partners (one case reported elsewhere in the country involved more than 150 searches on a single person), cameras that are notoriously easy to hack, and thin evidence that the technology solves crimes at all.

Many linked the cameras to the country’s broader drift toward what they called “techno-fascism” under President Donald Trump, pressing council members—many of whom posture as anti-Trump progressives—on how they had let the cameras go up in the first place.

Public comment was capped at three minutes per speaker. LPD Chief Robert Backus faced no such limit. His lengthy remarks amounted to a string of anecdotes about cases the cameras had supposedly helped solve, paired with a contradictory claim: that Flock cameras are no different from the license plate readers Lansing has used for two decades, yet somehow far more useful than those older ones ever were.

He also insisted the cameras “do not track people” and do not feed a national database—both false, and both, if true, would undercut the very benefits he was describing. His appearance wasn’t on the published agenda; even Kost said he hadn’t known the chief would be there.

📷Councilmember Ryan Kost confronting LPD Chief Robert Backus with evidence that his own license plate data was shared with other police departments. | City of Lansing

Council questions told a very different story than Backus’s opening remarks. Kost noted that the chief had repeatedly claimed “no one is accessing our data,” then produced a 2025 FOIA response from the Pittsboro, N.C., police department stating that “Lansing, Michigan PD has a ‘relationship of access, search enabled.’”
Backus responded that Lansing had “opted out” of data sharing in 2024. Kost pressed further: A search of his own license plate through public-records requests filed around the country had turned up a hit from Johnson County, Kansas—in 2025, a full year after the supposed opt-out. Backus repeated that sharing had ended in 2024 and suggested Flock itself might be to blame; Kost said he found it hard to believe Flock wasn’t “taking a peek” at data it manages on the city’s behalf.
Backus, in turn, said he found it hard to believe a company would lie about what it had accessed, pointing to Flock’s own assurance to Kost that his plate wasn’t in its system. Trusting a non-binding denial from a surveillance company over documentary evidence apparently presented little problem for the chief.

Kost closed by saying his real concern wasn’t Lansing PD’s current policies, but rather the certainty that any policy eventually gets violated and that the risk is too serious to take that chance.

Council Vice President Trini Pehlivanoglu then asked Backus to specify exactly when data sharing had ended; he said it happened in “stages” and was “all turned off,” without saying what the stages were or naming a date. Asked whether any loophole could still let data be shared against the city’s wishes, Backus said there was none.

Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez raised the cameras’ placement, noting they sit “disproportionately in our communities of color,” and asked whether Backus thought they also disproportionately criminalized the people who live there. His answer: Cameras go where traffic is heaviest, not where any particular community lives.

“So, I want to note in those locations the primary reason they’re there is because of the size of the thoroughfare, the traffic that’s involved there, and the idea that it’s—I mean, one of these cameras in a neighborhood is not gonna provide nearly the amount, if any, benefit to us,” he said.

“It has to be on a busy roadway. That’s the number one thing.” It would appear from this answer that Backus thinks Black and brown residents live only on busy roads.

Councilmember Adam Hussain later asked him to describe the correct way to use the technology; Backus explained that an officer can “hit search one time” and see everywhere a plate has been caught on camera—which is difficult to square with his earlier claim that the system doesn’t track people.

Asked for data on how often ALPRs had actually helped the department, Backus admitted, “I’ve done a bad job in actually documenting the times we’ve used it.”

Hours after the meeting began, the council finally voted 7–1 to approve the resolution, with only Council President Peter Spadafore opposed. The chamber erupted in cheers.

The resolution is non-binding—it’s now up to Mayor Andy Schor to actually cancel the contracts—and DeFlock Lansing says it won’t stop organizing until the council passes an outright ban on ALPRs. But the size of the turnout and the lopsided vote have energized organizers, who see the win as a foundation for the fights ahead. Readers who share DeFlock Lansing’s concerns are encouraged to join the campaign.

A step-by-step account of https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s response to the three takedown notices issued against its X account and posts.

1. Initial concerns regarding authenticity: Ordinarily, X's takedown notifications identify the law enforcement agency and the legal basis, but in our case the requesting authority was referred to as “Indian Police” and the legal basis as “Indian law."

2. Verification of email authenticity: We examined the underlying email header data to identify the originating IP address.

3. Seeking clarification from X: We wrote to X Corp and the platform’s support team seeking details of the law enforcement agency that had submitted the request, the statutory provisions invoked, and a copy of the underlying order or request.

4. Official Email to Delhi Police: We sent an email to the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, at the email address mentioned in the takedown notices, as well as the email addresses of other high-ranking officers, seeking clarification on whether Delhi Police has issued these orders.

5. Undelivered emails: Two of the three emails, including the one mentioned in the takedown orders, bounced back, stating that the “user doesn’t exist.”

6. Verification of X's takedown submission mechanisms: To further examine the authenticity of the two takedown requests, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 investigated the mechanisms available for submitting takedown requests to X and found that the Law Enforcement Request (LER) form lacks an authentication process to verify the identity of the sending authority.

7. Official Email Seeking clarification from X on the submission mechanism: We further wrote to X Corp seeking confirmation on whether the LER form was used to submit the takedown request against https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2. 

8. Follow-up verification of X's LER form: Following our letter, X added the authentication process to the form. 

9. Verification of the authority of the issuing officer: As per F. No. B/69/2025-Home-II/1246-1254, issued by the Home Department on 2 June 2026, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, who is identified as the issuing authority in the notices received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, is not among the officers authorised to issue takedown notices under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

10. Formal complaint to the IFSO Unit: We submitted a formal complaint to the IFSO Unit of the Delhi Police to seek clarification on whether the takedown orders were issued by them.

11. Discrepancy in the Email Address Listed on the Delhi Police Website: The Delhi Police has corrected the email ID, which was earlier flagged as incorrect by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2. This discrepancy further raises questions about the authenticity of the contact details provided in the notice and the authority from which it originated.
